output.headline: Labour’s manifesto author Ravinder Athwal brought in to strengthen Healey’s budget team
output.standfirst: Athwal is expected to arrive next week, a month before a critical budget, with the economy buffeted by high oil prices and rising borrowing costs; the move is likely to fuel early election speculation
output.bodyHtml:
Ravinder Athwal, the economist who wrote Labour’s 2024 manifesto, is taking on a senior role as an adviser to John Healey, bringing Treasury and Downing Street experience to the chancellor’s team in a move likely to fuel speculation about an early general election.

The chancellor is keen to strengthen his team before the critical budget on 28 October, as the economy is buffeted by high oil prices and rising government borrowing costs.

Healey has recruited Athwal as his senior special adviser from the business advisory group Flint Global, previously run by Andy Burnham’s chief of staff, the former Blair-era cabinet minister James Purnell.

Athwal, a Cambridge economics graduate, was closely associated with drawing up Labour’s manifesto and devising Keir Starmer’s five “missions”, which were meant to shape Labour’s approach to government. He worked as a senior economic adviser in Starmer’s Downing Street team but left after a year to join Flint Global.

Related: The man behind the manifesto: Labour’s quiet policy chief

A source close to Healey said: “Having Rav join John’s team as an experienced heavyweight economist at the Treasury ahead of this budget will be invaluable. His political nous will add to the special adviser team, providing John with guidance and counsel to the chancellor.”

Athwal’s presence on Healey’s team could be seen as a strength if the prime minister decides to draw up a fresh manifesto. Suggestions inside Westminster have been growing that Burnham is considering a snap general election after a recent bounce in the polls.

As well as strengthening the snap election rumours, Athwal’s arrival is likely to increase concerns among some in Labour that the Treasury’s instinctive caution is fuelling a “continuity Starmer” approach to economics.

Starmer’s team saw the pledge at the heart of the manifesto, not to increase income tax, national insurance or VAT, as key to Labour’s landslide victory two years ago. But it is widely agreed that it has restricted the party’s room for manoeuvre once in power.

People with knowledge of Athwal’s thinking suggest he has learned from the travails of Labour’s early months in office, however. One left-of-centre economist said: “I’d say he was at the more interesting and curious end of the Starmerite project.”

Before joining Labour, Athwal was a Treasury civil servant, rising to be head of growth strategy. One former colleague described him as “nice and clever – a good combination”.

After taking over at the Treasury in July, Healey hired Will Straw, who played a leading role in the remain campaign during the Brexit referendum, as his chief of staff; some of Rachel Reeves’s economic advisers, including Spencer Thompson, stayed on.

Reeves’s chief economic adviser, the former Clean Bandit violinist Neil Amin-Smith, who was closely involved in her plans to devolve more tax revenue to local leaders, has moved across to Burnham’s No 10.

Athwal is expected to arrive in post next week, a month before Healey’s first budget.

Healey faces a series of tough decisions, with inflation and borrowing costs expected to have wiped out at least half of the headroom Reeves had built up against Labour’s fiscal rules.

He has promised to maintain a “buffer against uncertainty”, though this is widely expected to be significantly smaller than the £24bn in the spring forecast.

Government sources say Healey wants this to be a “focused” budget, after Reeves used her two budgets as chancellor to increase taxes by £70bn a year. Depending on the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecasts, restoring the cushion in full would be likely to require large tax rises or spending cuts.

Key decisions about future tax and spending appear likely to be held over until a Treasury spending review next year, which will come after Burnham has set out his long-term priorities in a 10-year plan, expected after the budget.

Healey has made clear he does not intend to set a timetable at the budget for when the UK will spend 3% of gross domestic product on defence, for example – a target he insisted, when he resigned from Starmer’s government in June, must be met by 2030.

Treasury sources have said officials are working “at pace” on options for consumer support, as persistently high global oil and gas prices put hopes of a low-key budget under pressure and make it likely that the energy price cap, which determines UK consumer bills, will rise sharply in January.

That help is expected to fall far short of the costly universal approach taken by Liz Truss in 2022.

Flint Global was approached for comment.
output.progress: Treasury sources have said officials are working ‘at pace’ on options for consumer support, with the energy price cap likely to rise sharply in January.
